verdict: Choose (a), with one correction: `run_after` is not a priority mechanism and must not be used as one — it is a duty-cycle throttle, and priority comes from a yield check at the top of the handler. Implement `distill_memory` as a job kind that processes exactly ONE turn per job, checks for any queued non-distill job before doing any work and completes immediately as a no-op if it finds one, then always enqueues a single successor with `run_after = now() + cooldown`. Trigger and execution are both owned by the queue/executor: the trigger is the successor row's `run_after`, the execution is the executor's serial poll loop. No migration, no cron, no launcher change.
reasoning: AGAINST (a), the strongest case: the queue is actively working against you and every mitigation is voluntary cooperation layered on a scheduler that cannot express what you need. Your specific question — does `run_after` approximate deprioritisation? — has a worse answer than 'usually works': it PREDICTABLY LOSES. Ordering is `run_after asc, created_at asc` over rows already ready. A distill successor enqueued at T with delay D becomes ready at T+D; any WhatsApp job created after T+D has a strictly LATER `run_after`, so distill is claimed FIRST — not occasionally, but every single time a message arrives after the successor ripens. The window you asked about is real and it is not an edge case: it is every idle gap. And you cannot tune D away, because a D large enough to always lose is a D that never runs. Worse, `run_after` cannot touch the actual problem at all — head-of-line blocking is about work ALREADY IN FLIGHT, and claim ordering is irrelevant to a 55s extraction that has already started. Second charge against (a): it puts batch work back inside the component whose latency IS the product, which is the precise lesson of 26 Aug inverted, buying safety with discipline instead of isolation. Third and sharpest, from poller.py's own docstring: the in-process timeout does NOT kill the abandoned thread. A distill handler wedged on Ollama leaves a live thread still holding the model while the poller moves on to the next job — that is two concurrent Ollama consumers inside one process, the exact 26 Aug failure, invisible to the heartbeat because the heartbeat only sees processes. I accept (a) anyway, and the design must answer that third charge directly. AGAINST (b): it converts a memory-lag problem into an availability outage. The stop step always succeeds; the restart step is the one that fails, and its failure is SILENT — 'nobody is replying' is indistinguishable from 'nobody messaged'. Constraint 6 makes it worse: a wall clock firing into a sleeping laptop forces you to build missed-window catch-up, which is reimplementing, badly, the durable queue you already have. It also creates a second owner of the executor process that start_jarvis.py already supervises, and a 200-turn backlog means three-plus hours of deliberate, deliberate deafness. This is the worst of the three and it is not close. AGAINST (c): the launcher does not poll the queue and has no idle information; giving a process supervisor a Supabase client and a scheduling policy is a scope violation, in another lane's file, for a component Phase 4 rewrites. But the disqualifying flaw is epistemic, not organisational: 'idle' is a PREDICTION with no revocation path. There is no preemption, so a message arriving one second after the fire waits behind a full extraction, with the executor and a separate distill process both hitting one CPU-bound Ollama — 26 Aug's topology exactly. And it fails your own testing constraint: the safety property in (c) lives inside Ollama's request scheduler, which cannot be faked, so non-starvation can be hoped for but never PROVEN with fakes. It also only ever runs while a foreground terminal is open. On constraint 5, the heartbeat: (a) does NOT dismantle it. The guard lives in the CLI entry point and stays there, untouched, protecting the manual path. Its purpose was to stop a SECOND PROCESS competing for Ollama, and in-executor execution has exactly one process by construction — so in-executor serialisation is a legitimate substitute, not a bypass. What (a) does trade away is the guard's coarser intent ('system is live, do no batch work'), and it must pay for that with the finer-grained protections below, not with a `--force` flag. On constraint 8, retirement: (a) is cheapest by a wide margin. When the bus moves off-laptop the executor is still a pull worker, so the job kind keeps working unchanged; retiring it is deleting a registry entry and a self-enqueue line. (b) becomes actively wrong and leaves scheduler plumbing plus supervisor coupling to dismantle. (c) orphans code inside a component being rewritten in someone else's lane. On constraint 6, (a) needs NO missed-window handling at all: a laptop that sleeps simply means `run_after` passes, and the row is claimed on next boot. That is the single strongest practical argument for it. On constraint 9, no blueprint contradiction: Mem0 self-hosted, local Ollama, sqlite-vec and local-only extraction are all untouched, and a durable job kind is what the Phase 0 executor exists for. One requirement follows from the runbook's scheduled-CLI-job pattern: the handler and `tools/distill_memory.py` must share ONE library function; the CLI stays a working, guarded entry point rather than being replaced. DESIGN, precisely: (1) chunk = 1 turn, so worst-case in-flight blocking is one extraction, not N; (2) yield check first — a cheap SELECT for any queued job of another kind, and if one exists do zero extraction, re-enqueue, complete, which turns the ordering inversion's cost from 55s into one query plus one poll interval; (3) exactly one distill row in flight at any time, so the chain can never fan out and can never be more than one job ahead of a message; (4) when nothing is undistilled, still enqueue a successor at a long idle cooldown so the chain never dies and never needs re-seeding; (5) seed idempotently at executor startup only if no queued/running distill row exists; (6) register the handler with a timeout well above one extraction (e.g. 240s) AND give the Ollama client a shorter client-side timeout, so a wedged model raises rather than leaving an abandoned thread holding it — this is the answer to the third charge against (a); (7) never mark a turn distilled before extraction succeeds, preserving the CLI's existing invariant. WHAT THE TESTS MUST PROVE, all with fakes, no real Ollama, no live queue: (i) one-turn chunking — a fake store with M>1 undistilled turns yields exactly ONE extraction call per handler invocation, then returns; (ii) exactly one successor per run and never more than one queued/running distill row, asserted after repeated invocations; (iii) the yield — with a queued `whatsapp_webhook` row present, extraction call count is ZERO and the handler still re-enqueues; (iv) the anti-starvation bound — a fake JobRepository implementing the REAL ordering (`run_after asc, created_at asc`), a distill chain running, a WhatsApp job enqueued mid-chain at a controlled fake clock, driving `poll_once` in a loop, asserting the WhatsApp job reaches `done` within a BOUNDED number of polls and that at most one extraction occurred between its enqueue and its completion — assert a bound, never 'eventually'; (v) the inversion itself, encoded deliberately — construct the case where the distill row's `run_after` is strictly older, assert distill IS claimed first, then assert the WhatsApp job completes on the next poll anyway; this test is what makes deleting the yield check fail CI, and without it the yield is a comment; (vi) idle tick — zero undistilled turns produces zero extractions and a successor at the long cooldown; (vii) sleep catch-up — a fake clock jumped hours forward claims the stale row ONCE and does not burst to make up missed ticks; (viii) failure isolation — extraction raising leaves the turn undistilled and leaves exactly one distill row queued, with no orphaned and no duplicated chain; (ix) timeout config — assert the registered `timeout_seconds` exceeds one extraction and that the client-side timeout is strictly shorter than it. Shared-interface note for the report: `DEFAULT_HANDLERS` in executor/poller.py gains a key, so every test double or assertion that enumerates its keys must be named in the lane report even where the lane cannot edit it.
what_would_change_this: A measurement showing a single-turn extraction is not reliably bounded — a p99 well above ~55s, or extraction that is one uninterruptible call routinely running into minutes. That would make in-executor execution unbounded head-of-line blocking on the reply path, and out-of-process isolation with an interruptible batch would beat it. Also flipping: the user granting the priority-column migration, which makes the yield check unnecessary and (a) strictly cleaner; or evidence that a live reply's own Ollama call is already slow enough that adding one extraction plus a poll interval pushes total reply latency past what WhatsApp conversation tolerates, in which case the correct answer is that NO concurrent distillation is safe and the mechanism must be a hard mutual-exclusion window after all.
_question:
Pick the scheduling mechanism for tools/distill_memory.py, and argue against each candidate before you decide. I want the strongest case AGAINST each of the three, not a ranking. Then commit to one.

Candidates:
(a) A self-re-enqueuing low-priority executor job kind. A `distill_memory` job processes N turns, then enqueues its own successor, so live replies interleave between chunks instead of waiting out a whole batch.
(b) A scheduled window. Cleanly stop the executor, distill, restart it.
(c) A launcher-owned idle-window trigger. tools/start_jarvis.py notices an idle period and fires distillation itself.

Hard constraints, all real and all verified in this repo:

1. Ollama is a SINGLE SERIAL RESOURCE on this laptop, CPU-only. Any batch pass drives the exact same local model live WhatsApp replies need. This is not theoretical: a backfill starved eight inbound WhatsApp messages on 26 Aug 2026 (docs/history/whatsapp-reply-failures.md). That incident is why executor/heartbeat.py exists.

2. Mem0 fact extraction costs ~55s per turn. An embedding costs ~0.5s. That is ~250x, and it is why extraction was taken off the reply path entirely after failing on 100% of live messages.

3. The executor is a SINGLE SERIAL POLL LOOP. executor/poller.py claims and runs ONE job at a time, with a default 5s idle poll interval and an in-process thread timeout that does NOT kill the abandoned thread. A distill job holding Ollama for 55s blocks the loop for 55s. N turns per job means N x 55s of blockage.

4. THE QUEUE HAS NO PRIORITY COLUMN. This is the sharpest constraint on (a). claim_next_job in db/migrations/0002_job_retries.sql orders strictly `order by run_after asc, created_at asc` over rows where `status='queued' and run_after <= now()`. So a distill job that is OLDER than an incoming WhatsApp job gets claimed FIRST. "Low priority" is not expressible today. Adding a priority column is a schema migration against the LIVE Supabase database, which needs explicit user approval and is a hard stop for me - so treat it as a COST of (a), not a free move.
   Specifically answer: can `run_after` scheduling alone approximate deprioritisation without a migration? If a distill job's successor is enqueued with run_after = now() + delay, does that make it reliably lose the race to a WhatsApp job, or does it merely usually-work? Note the tie-break is created_at, and a WhatsApp job created at T has run_after = T (immediate), while a distill successor enqueued at T with a delay has run_after = T+delay. Is there any window where the distill job still wins - for example when the queue was idle and the distill successor became ready before the WhatsApp job was created, making the distill row strictly older by run_after? Is "usually works" acceptable given constraint 1's incident?

5. THE HEARTBEAT REFUSAL ALREADY EXISTS. executor/heartbeat.py makes distill_memory.py refuse to start while the executor is polling (timestamp file, 600s staleness window, --force to override). Candidate (a) runs distillation INSIDE the executor, which means the guard must be bypassed for that path. Does bypassing it dismantle the exact protection that stopped the 26 Aug failure from recurring? Or is in-executor serialisation a legitimate substitute for the guard, because the executor cannot run two jobs at once anyway and the guard only ever existed to stop a SECOND process competing for Ollama?

6. THE LAPTOP IS NOT ALWAYS ON. Nothing receives messages while it is off. Any wall-clock schedule (cron, Windows Task Scheduler, "3am nightly") fires into a machine that may be asleep. Missed windows must be HANDLED, not assumed away. Candidate (b) in particular: who stops and restarts the executor, and what happens if the machine is asleep at window time, or if the restart step fails and the executor stays down silently - i.e. the failure mode is "JARVIS is deaf and nobody notices"?

7. Candidate (c) touches tools/start_jarvis.py, which is owned by a DIFFERENT LANE. I cannot edit it; I can only specify the change for another agent to merge. That is a coordination cost, not a blocker. Also: start_jarvis.py is a foreground process supervisor that already brings up Ollama check, bus, tunnel, Meta re-point and executor in order and shuts them down together on Ctrl+C. Is adding idle-detection to a process supervisor a scope violation, and does the launcher even have the information to know the queue is idle? It does not poll the queue today.

8. Phase 4 eventually moves the bus off the laptop, which changes this calculus entirely. Which mechanism is CHEAPEST TO RETIRE when that happens?

9. Blueprint constraint: docs/blueprint.md specifies Mem0 self-hosted against local Ollama + sqlite-vec, with extraction local-only (NIM is geo-blocked from Pakistan, Gemini's free tier may train on prompts). The blueprint's runbook does describe scheduled CLI-agent jobs as an ongoing pattern. Architecture in the blueprint is a DECISION, not a claim - if your winner contradicts it, say so explicitly and I will stop and report rather than substitute.

Decide one. If your answer is a hybrid, name precisely which mechanism owns the TRIGGER and which owns the EXECUTION, because a hybrid that is really "all three" is not something I can implement. Also state, concretely, what the implementation must prove in tests to show a distill pass cannot starve a live reply - I must use fakes, no real Ollama and no live queue.
